varieties.name: Strap-leaf (A. vittariifolium)
varieties.note: Ribbon leaves a metre and more long, hanging straight down from a short stem. An epiphyte from the wet forests of Colombia and Ecuador: in the wild its roots sit in leaf litter on a branch, not in soil, so the pot wants bark and the roots want air. Grown for the leaves; the flowers are small and the berries, which take months, are the show. It is a climber by habit and will do better given something to hang from than a shelf that bends its leaves.

varieties.name: Flamingo flower (A. andraeanum)
varieties.note: The florist's anthurium, with the lacquered red or white spathe. The toughest of this group indoors and the one that tolerates an ordinary pot and ordinary air; it stops flowering in a dim corner long before it looks unhappy.

varieties.name: Clarinervium
varieties.note: Thick velvet heart with bone-white veins. A rock-dweller rather than a tree-dweller, so it takes a slightly heavier mix than the strap-leaf kinds, and it marks if water sits on the leaf.

varieties.name: Crystallinum
varieties.note: Like the clarinervium but thinner and faster, with a crystalline sheen along the veins. Wants the humidity kept up; the new leaves crisp at the edge while opening if the air is dry.

varieties.name: Queen anthurium (A. warocqueanum)
varieties.note: Long velvet pendant leaves, the hardest of these to keep. Wants high humidity, moving air and a mix that is nearly all bark; it is the first to rot and the first to complain about a dry room.

varieties.name: King anthurium (A. veitchii)
varieties.note: Pleated, corrugated pendant leaves. Epiphytic like the strap-leaf, and like it does better hung than stood.

watering.label: Water through and let the top of the bark dry, no further. These are epiphytes: the roots want air as much as water, and they rot sooner than they wilt

drainage.label: Chunky bark with perlite and charcoal, barely any soil. Water should run straight through and the pot must never stand in what came out

young: Too dark for a young plant. A rooted cutting has nothing in reserve and simply stops.
Dim. The first leaves come up short and never reach their length.
A little short for a young plant. It holds what it has and adds nothing.
established: Too dark. New leaves come up smaller each round, which is how this genus fades out.
Dim. It keeps its leaves and stops making them; the flowering kinds stop flowering first.
A little short. It holds, but it will not put out a new leaf.

young: Too much for a young plant. The newest leaf pales and its edge goes thin.
Well past what a young plant takes. New leaves crisp as they unfurl.
Far too much for a young plant. A soft new leaf burns through in an afternoon.
established: Too much. The leaf yellows overall and loses its depth of colour.
Burning. Dry tan patches spread where the sun falls and do not heal.
Far too much. These grow under a canopy; a bare window scorches them through.
